snippet.textDisplay:
Voice mode does not work the way it needs to yet. 
It's not "hearing" us. It's transcribing sounds into text, and then sending that text as a prompt to the normal AI, that then writes a response in text, that is sent to a text-to-voice model...

If you're trying to show someone what AI can do using voice mode, there is no difference between a 30 year old male and his daughters pre-teen voice. It thinks all words spoken are the same user.

It needs work. Maybe even ground up...but I don't have a better way, just recognize our current way doesn't work unless you're alone in silence. 

We also need to shorten Grok's desire to explain so deeply. That, "Sorry, I don....I don't have real time data." hesitation was voice mode trying to pick up a new prompt. 
Even if we figure out how to allow AI to actually hear individual voices, the current LLM's can't handle multiple prompts to a single response. 
I.e. "Grok, I'd like to know the weather for today but first, where is the" send, but then before the response send "Sorry, I fat fingered the send button. Where is the bathroom?" 
Most AI will forget about the weather request entirely. This is a major problem for voice mode imo...but again, Im just some dude on the internet. Not a proper AI researcher/engineer

I don’t think people get the idea of real time processing of info vs a robot being programmed to do a thing. Atlas is preprogrammed to do those actions and then they run it through a lot. Still massively amazing what they can do but having a bot understand you and in real time figure out what it needs to do is the hard part. For us doing backflips and parkour is harder, for bots I actually think folding laundry is harder than running and jumping and dancing. We have to have athleticism and skill to do the parkour stuff they alreuad have in built athleticism it’s the decision making and vision system and machine learning part that’s a lot harder and it’s actually massively complicated to fold laundry vs doing a flip or jumping which is very hard but once you’ve got stability down and movement you can kind of do that but the next stage of learning to think a lot deeper and contextually is harder which you need in order to know these how to fold a thing correctly and how to wash it and choose settings for it and the dexterity needed is pretty high actually for very finally grabbing and exact piece of the fabric and folding it over in pattern and then doing that in different ways for each piece. 

And similarly it’s challenging to understanding human speech and context and do actions. Though it does seem like it can do it a bit faster than this. It can dance and do all kinds of stuff actually I think they just keep it in basic mode for safety around people and to make it less likely to break. But bots are still pretty early in development for actual use. They’re kind of there but not quite there, it’s like the eighties for cellphones or maybe the nineties. They kind of work like the eighties but are costly and can’t fully do it all yet. By the nineties they were pretty affordable and worked pretty well and then the next decade they had commercial smartphones. So we may actually be more like the nineties right now though price is pretty scaled up and really in terms of production it’s more the eighties.

snippet.textDisplay:
The military has a few systems like this. 
The issue is motion tracking is very difficult in a battlefield and humans need to say okay before you let your crow system start firing so it doesn't make mistakes. 
Drones are very small and can be made to be less detectable or out of range. 
Accurate tracking of a small object that flies in full XYZ and can hover is very complicated. 
The round leaving the barrel has a delay and must lead the target. Very easily you can program a drone to know how to pattern maneuver to avoid getting hit because the system won't be quick enough to lead the shot. 
If the distance is close enough the gun will win but if the drone has a large enough explosive it won't matter. Avoid the gun until close enough to cause casualties and then detonate. With danger areas of 200m and deadly at 60m and fatal at 15m they don't exactly have to hit their target but the gun has to hit them. Huge disadvantage to defensive shooting. 

We need a weapon with limitless ammunition or a weapon with a continuous beam. 
Lasers or microwaves are going to be more effective than projectile weapons but I personally haven't seen any in use. 
Crown dispersion microwaves aren't going to be enough. 
Lasers have very limited range. The atmosphere and lasers just don't refract well together. 

Super cool turret. 
Wish I could build something this elaborate and smart. 
My robot arms and 3d printers are a far cry. The skill of making this identify and track objects is awesome. 
I know adafruit had some chips that were designed to handle this task but beyond my programming skills

snippet.textDisplay:
@IhavenoarmsbutImustGOON-n6e Advanced Infrared (IR) sensors cannot see through thick sheets of material because thick materials block infrared radiation, which is the heat signature the sensors detect. While thin, opaque plastics can be somewhat transparent to infrared, thicker substances like concrete, walls, or even significant layers of fabric will block the heat signature, making it impossible for the sensor to see through them to the person behind. 

Why it doesn't work:

Infrared blocking materials:

Materials like thick glass, walls, and metal foil block infrared radiation, preventing the sensor from seeing the heat source. 

Limitations of the technology:

Thermal sensors detect temperature differences. If a thick sheet is placed in front of a person, the sheet will absorb and block the person's body heat, and the sensor will only register the temperature of the sheet itself, not the heat from the person. 

Conductivity:

Electrically conducting materials, such as aluminum foil, are particularly effective at blocking infrared radiation. 

What can be seen:

Thin materials:

Very thin, non-conductive materials like certain plastic bags can allow some infrared to pass through, revealing what's behind them. 

Environmental heat signatures:

A thermal camera can detect temperature differences in the environment, such as a hot or cold pipe within a wall, but not the heat of solid objects through the wall itself. 

IN SUMMERY:  any significant, thick, or conducting material will obscure the heat signature of a person from an IR sensor.

snippet.textDisplay:
It's trippy, just reflecting on it and where we've come today. A thing moving by itself, a thing with no soul or actual life, walking over to put something in the trash, or have the complexity of a human hand to grip a fridge handle and open it. 

Uncanny, that it looks human, does human things but isn't human. It's easy to take it for granted and just think of the tech behind it and it's functions doing those things. But when you take a step back and look at what we accomplished or created, it's wild. Something that moves itself and it's 'own hands' without anyone moving it, yet it has no life... 

Trippy, almost ghostly..
